name: Taskflow
workload: Large-scale machine-learning task graph (heterogeneous CPU+GPU pipeline) executed via Taskflow's executor vs. oneTBB's FlowGraph on a 40-CPU, 4-GPU machine
claimed_speedup: up to 29% faster runtime, 1.5x less memory, and 1.9x higher throughput than oneTBB on the ML workload
hardware: 40 CPUs, 4 GPUs (specific CPU/GPU model not stated in the abstract)
tradeoffs: Header-only but requires C++17/20; DAG/graph-based task model differs from raw std::async/std::thread call sites, so adopting it means restructuring code around tf::Taskflow/tf::Executor; larger API surface than a simple thread pool.
caveats: This benchmark measures Taskflow against Intel oneTBB, not against std::async/std::thread/std::future directly (oneTBB is itself already catalogued separately as a faster-than-std library, so this shows Taskflow beating another fast library, one step removed from the raw std baseline). GitHub's license detector reports NOASSERTION for this repo, but the LICENSE file text is the standard MIT license. Compiler/flags for the ML benchmark are not stated in the abstract, only CPU/GPU counts, so tier is capped at B rather than A. The repo's own benchmarks/ directory (thread_pool, graph_traversal, wavefront, etc.) additionally compares Taskflow to OpenMP tasking and TBB FlowGraph, not to std::async/thread.

name: Boost.Fiber
workload: skynet microbenchmark (ported from atemerev/skynet): spawn 10 threads-of-execution recursively until 1,000,000 total actors/fibers are created (only 10,000 for std::thread/std::async/pthread due to resource exhaustion); each returns its ordinal number, summed back up to the root; average time-per-unit measured with std::chrono::high_resolution_clock
claimed_speedup: fiber (16C/32T, work-stealing scheduler, tcmalloc): 0.05-0.09 microseconds/fiber vs std::thread 52-73 microseconds/thread and std::async 106-122 microseconds/thread over 10,000 units (~600-1400x lower time-per-unit; derived from page data)
hardware: dual Intel Xeon E5-2620v4 2.2GHz, 16 cores/32 threads, 64GB RAM, Linux x86_64
stars_or_usage: 511 stars on the standalone mirror; ships as part of the Boost C++ Libraries collection used industry-wide
tradeoffs: Cooperative user-space scheduling: a blocking syscall or CPU-bound fiber can stall all fibers on its worker thread unless paired with async I/O (e.g. Boost.Asio integration); best numbers require a non-default allocator (tcmalloc) and a work-stealing scheduler configuration; different programming model (fiber-per-task) than raw std::thread/std::async call sites.
caveats: Numbers come from Boost's own project documentation (first party), though the benchmark code itself (performance/thread/skynet_std.cpp and the fiber counterpart in the same repo) is public and the compiler/flags/hardware are all stated, meeting the tier-A bar despite the source being first-party. The raw ratio (>50x) looks extreme, but it is explained by mechanism (fiber creation/context switch avoids syscalls and stack-guard-page setup that std::thread/std::async incur) rather than a flawed methodology; std::thread could only be tested at 10,000 units instead of 1,000,000 due to OS resource exhaustion, so the two are not run at identical scale. Measurements were taken with gcc-6.3.1, an old compiler (circa 2017); the fiber library and hardware landscape have moved on since, and the doc gives no indication the numbers were re-run on newer toolchains.

name: utl::parallel (UTL ThreadPool)
workload: Four microbenchmark scenarios, 1000 tasks each: (1) small non-recursive tasks busy-waiting 0-100us, (2) large non-recursive tasks busy-waiting 1000-3000us, (3) shallow recursive tasks (0-100us with 70% chance of spawning+awaiting one more such task), (4) deep recursive tasks (0-100us with 49% chance of spawning+awaiting two more such tasks, averaging ~50 subtasks); reports ms/op and op/s relative to a serial baseline
claimed_speedup: Small non-recursive: utl::parallel::ThreadPool 573.3% vs std::async() 214.0% of serial speed (~2.7x faster than std::async, derived from page data). Large non-recursive: 597.0% vs 564.2% (~1.06x, roughly tied). Shallow recursive: 583.0% vs 161.1% (~3.6x faster than std::async; BS::thread_pool and progschj/ThreadPool deadlock entirely on this workload). Deep recursive: 565.1% vs 154.7% (~3.65x faster than std::async, derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Uses a custom future type instead of std::future so recursive awaiting doesn't deadlock, so it is not a drop-in std::future replacement; ships as one module inside a larger multi-module header-only utility collection (UTL) rather than a standalone package; explicitly a niche tool for recursive/scatter-gather workloads, not a general vendor-optimized scheduler like TBB/OpenMP.
caveats: Author explicitly disclaims superiority over vendor-optimized frameworks (OpenMP/TBB). On large non-recursive tasks the advantage over std::async almost disappears (~1.06x) since thread-creation overhead is amortized; the large speedups are concentrated in small-task and recursive-task scenarios, exactly where std::async's per-call thread-spawn cost dominates. Benchmarked on a single consumer laptop CPU (Ryzen 5 5600H), not server-class hardware; this is the project's own README benchmark with no independent third-party reproduction found, though code, compiler, flags, and CPU model are all public and stated (meets Tier A bar on reproducibility grounds). Library itself is small (336 stars) and young.
